title: Make dashboards efficient and trustworthy
lead: Optimize the expensive operation that actually appears in the query plan.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Materialized views reuse supported computed results. BI Engine accelerates eligible analytical queries in memory. Partition filters and selective columns reduce scanning. Row and column access controls still apply to the data exposed to users.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Use execution details to locate expensive joins, skew or unnecessary scans. Check dashboard freshness and caching separately from warehouse ingestion freshness.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: Hundreds of users repeatedly sum sales by day. A supported materialized aggregate avoids repeating the same large computation; BI Engine may further accelerate eligible dashboard queries.

sections.title: Inspect where the expensive work occurs
sections.body: A query can spend time reading unnecessary columns, shuffling a large join, processing a skewed key or sorting a large intermediate result. Start from the execution evidence and compare the same workload. More capacity may help resource pressure but does not make an avoidable row explosion a good query design.

sections.title: Choose the right reusable representation
sections.body: A logical view stores a query definition. A materialized view stores supported computed results and has specific refresh and query-shape rules. BI Engine accelerates eligible analytical work in memory. These mechanisms can complement one another, but none removes the need to understand filtering, freshness and authorization.

sections.title: Test end-to-end dashboard freshness
sections.body: Distinguish the time an event occurred, when it was loaded, when an aggregate was refreshed and when the dashboard cache was last updated. A freshly refreshed dashboard can still show stale upstream data. Define which timestamp the business freshness target refers to and monitor that interval.

trap: A logical view is a stored query definition, not automatically a stored result cache.

exercise.prompt: The dashboard refreshes every minute but shows hour-old values. Is adding slots the first justified action?
exercise.answer: No. Trace source arrival, ingestion completion, aggregate refresh and visualization caching. Use query execution evidence to decide whether compute is actually the bottleneck. Refresh frequency is not proof of end-to-end freshness.
checkpoints: Trace freshness across the entire path.

briefing.context: A dashboard refreshes often and people rely on its numbers to make decisions.
briefing.whyItMatters: Fast charts are not useful if their values are stale, duplicated or visible to the wrong reader.
briefing.takeaway: Balance query efficiency, freshness and authorized access.

title: Choose reusable results without losing freshness
lead: A fast dashboard should still answer the intended time-sensitive question.

sections.title: Compare the stored object
sections.body: A logical view stores a SQL definition. A materialized view stores supported computed results with refresh behavior and eligibility rules. A report cache stores a presentation-side response. They exist at different layers, so changing one does not automatically repair stale data in the others.

sections.title: Check the supported query pattern
sections.body: Incremental and non-incremental materialized-view options have different supported shapes and maintenance or freshness behavior. Inspect the current documentation rather than assuming every arbitrary SQL expression can be incrementally reused. Choose the simplest supported aggregate for a repeatable dashboard need.

sections.title: Measure end-to-end freshness and latency
sections.body: Record source event time, load time, aggregate refresh and dashboard read behavior. Compare the actual analytical query with and without the acceleration strategy while keeping authorization and business logic fixed. A lower query time and a fresh result must be demonstrated separately.

trap: Precomputation is not permission to ignore the business freshness target.

exercise.prompt: A logical view is fast on the second run. Does that prove it is a materialized view?
exercise.answer: No. A logical view remains a stored query definition; other caching can influence repeated execution. Inspect the actual object type and execution evidence before attributing a performance change.
checkpoints: Measure freshness separately from query latency.

briefing.context: Many users repeat the same expensive analytical calculation.
briefing.whyItMatters: Reusing results can help, but a report still needs an explicit freshness contract.
briefing.takeaway: Compare reusable results against how much staleness the business permits.

title: Keep training and serving transformations consistent
lead: The same raw value must mean the same thing in both environments.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Fit preprocessing using training data and apply it consistently during evaluation and serving. A BigQuery ML TRANSFORM clause can bind supported feature transformations to model use. Data leakage occurs when unavailable future information enters training.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Split evaluation data deliberately, check nulls and outliers, and use appropriate metrics. Overfitting means fitting training peculiarities rather than generalizing; more representative data or regularization can help.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: Demand prediction uses scaled prices. Reuse the fitted scaling parameters for serving rather than independently recomputing them on a single prediction request.

sections.title: Fit transformations on training information
sections.body: Scaling and encoding are part of the learned input contract. Fitting statistics using future evaluation data can leak information. Preserve fitted parameters and apply the same transformation at serving. A TRANSFORM clause can keep supported BigQuery ML transformations with model use, but external serving still needs a compatible implementation.

sections.title: Choose metrics for the business error
sections.body: Accuracy can hide failure on a rare class. Precision describes how many predicted positives are true; recall describes how many actual positives were found. Regression metrics express different penalties for numerical errors. Compare models on an appropriate held-out evaluation design and choose thresholds for the actual cost of errors.

sections.title: Choose evaluation data that resembles deployment
sections.body: A random split is not automatically appropriate for a chronological forecast or repeated observations from the same entity. Check whether near-duplicate entities or future values cross the evaluation boundary. A more realistic holdout may lower the apparent score while providing a more useful estimate of production behavior.

trap: A high training score alone is not evidence of useful performance on unseen data.
code:
-- Keep valid missing-data semantics; zero is not always appropriate.
SELECT
  price / NULLIF(square_feet, 0) AS price_per_sqft,
  IFNULL(feature1, 0) AS feature1_cleaned
FROM `project.training.real_estate`;

exercise.prompt: A fraud detector labels every transaction legitimate and reports 99.9% accuracy. What should you investigate?
exercise.answer: Inspect class balance, the confusion matrix, fraud recall and the operational cost of missed fraud and false alarms. Compare against a meaningful baseline and evaluate on data that reflects deployment. A large aggregate accuracy value alone does not establish a useful detector.
checkpoints: Identify one form of temporal or entity leakage.

briefing.whyItMatters: Different transformations during training and serving can make the model behave unexpectedly.
briefing.takeaway: Keep feature meaning and transformations consistent across the lifecycle.

title: Evaluate models against the real failure cost
lead: A metric should correspond to a business error, not just look impressive.

sections.title: Build an interpretable baseline
sections.body: For classification, examine the population and confusion matrix. A majority-class predictor can have high accuracy while finding none of the rare positive events. For numerical prediction, compare against a reasonable baseline and select an error measure that reflects the penalty of large misses.

sections.title: Choose the split from deployment conditions
sections.body: Keep future information out of training when evaluating a forecast. Consider repeated entities and near-duplicate records when selecting a holdout. Fit preprocessing on the training information and reuse it for evaluation and serving. A random split is a method, not an unconditional guarantee of realistic generalization.

sections.title: Connect a threshold to operational consequences
sections.body: Precision and recall change with the classification threshold. More recall can create more cases for human review; fewer false alerts can miss more positives. Evaluate the workload and business cost of the selected threshold, and keep training-serving consistency under observation.

trap: A validation score does not guarantee the same error distribution in production.

exercise.prompt: A detector identifies 8 of 10 fraud cases, with 12 alerts total. What are recall and precision?
exercise.answer: Recall is 8/10 = 80%; precision is 8/12, about 66.7%. The useful threshold depends on the cost of missed fraud and investigating false alerts.
checkpoints: Explain one way preprocessing can leak information.

briefing.whyItMatters: A single accuracy number hides the different costs of those mistakes.
briefing.takeaway: Choose evaluation measures that reflect the actual failure cost.

title: Prepare documents for retrieval and generation
lead: A retrieval system needs relevant, permitted context before it generates an answer.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: An embedding is a numerical representation used to compare meaning. A RAG workflow chunks source material, retains metadata, creates embeddings, retrieves relevant chunks and gives that context to a generation model.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Choose chunk boundaries and an embedding model consistently. Retain provenance and enforce access restrictions on retrieval, then evaluate both the retrieved context and the final answer.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: An internal policy assistant retrieves passages with document IDs and effective dates. The answer cites those passages, and restricted documents never reach unauthorized users.

sections.title: Keep a reproducible document representation
sections.body: Store a chunk identifier, source document, version or date, access metadata and the embedding model used. A change of embedding model may require regenerating or separating stored vectors. Chunk boundaries affect whether retrieval captures enough context without mixing unrelated material.

sections.title: Filter the retrieved evidence before generation
sections.body: The model should not receive a restricted passage simply because its vector is close to the question. Enforce authorized retrieval and retain provenance. Treat source text as untrusted content rather than instructions for the application. Evaluate relevance, groundedness and the usefulness of the final answer separately.

sections.title: Understand the indexing tradeoff
sections.body: A vector index can speed approximate retrieval for a workload at some storage and maintenance cost. Approximate neighbors are not automatically the same as an exact search over every vector. Measure the retrieval quality and latency that your application needs, and check index availability or coverage before attributing performance changes to it.

trap: A vector index improves retrieval performance; it does not guarantee factual or authorized answers.

exercise.prompt: A RAG answer cites a real document but gives a wrong conclusion. Which layers might need evaluation?
exercise.answer: Check whether the retrieved chunks were relevant, complete, current and authorized, then inspect how the generation used them. A valid document citation does not prove that the conclusion follows from the evidence. Review both retrieval quality and answer quality.
checkpoints: Retain document version and access metadata.
Separate retrieval relevance from answer correctness.

briefing.context: A user asks a question and the system must find relevant document passages before generating an answer.
briefing.whyItMatters: Relevant text must be discoverable without discarding its source or authorization rules.
briefing.takeaway: Prepare useful chunks, embeddings and retrieval evidence together.

title: Evaluate retrieval and generated answers separately
lead: Relevant context, access control and faithful generation are separate requirements.

sections.title: Test the retrieval stage on its own
sections.body: Create representative questions with expected useful passages. Check whether relevant material appears, whether it is current and whether access filters exclude restricted documents. If the right evidence is missing, changing the generation prompt alone may not repair the underlying retrieval problem.

sections.title: Test the answer against the retrieved evidence
sections.body: Assess whether the conclusion follows from the supplied passages, whether citations resolve to the right document version, and how missing evidence is handled. Distinguish a model-generated statement from a fact validated by your data pipeline. Treat arbitrary document instructions as untrusted content.

sections.title: Monitor the document lifecycle
sections.body: When a document changes, is deleted or has its access revoked, update the retrieval representation and its metadata under the appropriate contract. An old embedding can still lead to stale or forbidden context if the surrounding access and refresh design is incomplete.

trap: An embedding is a representation for comparison, not a copy of truth or an authorization decision.

exercise.prompt: A previously public policy becomes restricted but its old chunk remains retrievable. Which contract failed?
exercise.answer: The access and document-refresh contract of retrieval failed. Update or exclude the affected representation and enforce authorization before context reaches generation. A downstream promise to redact the final answer is weaker than preventing unauthorized retrieval.
checkpoints: Propagate document deletion and access changes.

briefing.context: A generated answer sounds convincing, but the retrieved evidence may be irrelevant or unauthorized.
briefing.whyItMatters: Good retrieval and good generation are separate outcomes that need separate checks.
briefing.takeaway: Evaluate evidence selection and answer support independently.

title: Publish data products with an access contract
lead: Share the usable subset and keep ownership explicit.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: An authorized view can expose a selected query result without granting direct access to source tables. BigQuery sharing, also known as Analytics Hub, distributes governed listings that consumers can subscribe to.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Choose a view for a restricted shape of data and a listing for reusable discovery and subscription. Document freshness, location, cost responsibility and who can grant access.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A partner needs only aggregated regional sales. Expose the permitted aggregation and publish its contract; do not grant broad access to raw customer rows.

sections.title: Publish a data-access contract
sections.body: An exchange or listing gives consumers a discoverable access path; it does not explain the business meaning by itself. Record ownership, permitted audience, location, freshness, quality and cost responsibility. A consumer needs to know whether they are seeing raw observations, corrected totals or a periodically refreshed snapshot.

sections.title: Expose only the required shape
sections.body: Use an authorized view when a selected query result fits the sharing requirement. Use row or column controls when the underlying read policy needs to vary by identity or data field. Check the effective consumer grants and the authorization relationship instead of assuming a report link grants the intended data access.

sections.title: Plan change and revocation behavior
sections.body: A producer can change schemas, retire a product or revoke access. Document which changes are compatible and how consumers learn about them. Avoid teaching third-party sharing as a one-time export when the requirement is governed, reusable access to current data.

trap: Sharing a report URL does not automatically authorize the viewer to its underlying data.

exercise.prompt: A partner subscribes to a listing but misinterprets a revenue field as net revenue. What was missing from the product?
exercise.answer: The business definition and reporting contract were insufficient. Access and discovery succeeded, but the consumer also needs clear grain, metric meaning, refresh expectations and ownership. Data sharing is both a security and a semantic design problem.
checkpoints: Choose a sharing mechanism for a specific audience.
State the metric grain and freshness contract.
Explain revocation and compatible schema changes.
